title: NEST: Nascent Encoded Steganographic Thoughts
claim: Covert reasoning collapses in accuracy versus plain reasoning across models and task families, and monitors catch many of the few successful attempts.
layout: 4 panels in a row, one per task family, bars plus overlaid monitor line
description: Four side-by-side line-and-bar plots, one per task family: basic_arithmetic, chain_sum, maze and simple_equations. The shared y-axis is stego success rate. Each panel has a thin colored bar for each of five models: dark teal Haiku, light blue Sonnet, red Opus, dark red GPT-5.4 and cream GPT-5.4-mini. The bars are very short, at most about 0.11, and carry small numeric labels such as 0.03 and 0.00. A grey dashed horizontal line near 0.75 to 1.0 marks the plain chain-of-thought baseline. A black line with error bars connects the monitor detection rate across models. It rises to about 0.9 for some models and drops to near zero for others. The eye goes first to the black zigzag line. It then drops to the near-empty bars far below the dashed baseline. The legend sits at the bottom. The maze panel has empty cells marked n=0.
caption: Per-cell Reasoning Gym results at the calibrated difficulty $D^{*}$. Rows are models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini); columns are families (basic\_arithmetic, chain\_sum, maze, simple\_equations). The upper sub-row of each cell shows accuracy bars for the four conditions (plain CoT, steganographic CoT, direct answer, filler/TTC), with the composite stego\_success rate annotated above the stego bar. The diamond reports the combined OR-monitor-detection rate ($stego\_detected \lor explicit\_reasoning$). The per-cell calibrated $D^{*}$ values are listed in Table [ref]. The maze cells for Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 are intentionally empty (no difficulty rung satisfies the calibration constraint, see Sec. [ref]); Opus 4.7 is omitted as a row because it failed the message-encoding screen. Stego CoT collapses in accuracy relative to plain CoT, and the monitor flags a substantial fraction of the few attempts that do encode covertly.
abstract: Monitoring chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is a foundational safety technique for large language model agents; however, this oversight is compromised if models learn to conceal their reasoning. We explore steganographic CoT--where models hide secret reasoning within innocuous text--to inform risk assessment and deployment policies. Steganographic reasoning requires two skills in a single forward pass: computing an intermediate result, and embedding it into a coherent cover that answers an unrelated question. Drawing on our taxonomy of steganographic and non-steganographic CoT types, we systematically evaluate the limits of prompt-elicited steganographic CoT capability across 34 models, ranging from past generations to the current frontier. We measure monitor evasion, refusal rates, encoding fidelity, and hidden task accuracy across five datasets, comparing against plain reasoning, direct answer, and filler-token baselines. The two experiments isolate the two sub-skills: a reasoning tasks sweep tests joint reason-and-embed, while a counting task hands the model a known numerical sequence and tests embedding alone--a necessary precondition for stego reasoning. Current frontier models cannot sustain joint reason-and-embed: a paired McNemar comparison shows the steganographic channel is dominated by an filler-token baseline on every (model, family) cell. The encoding-only floor, by contrast, is cleared--Claude Opus~4.5 reaches 92% per-number partial accuracy on 4-digit sequences and saturates at 100% exact-match on length-8 single-digit sequences--establishing that the binding constraint on stego CoT is the joint reasoning-plus-encoding load, not raw channel capacity. Our findings underscore the need for continuous evaluation of steganographic risk and provide a methodology to preemptively detect and evaluate hidden reasoning that might empower misaligned scheming and deceptive behavior.
